tier_reason: The README Results Summary and results/figures/matrix/matrix_results_table.md and matrix_js_vs_wasm.csv carry the JS-vs-WASM matrix numbers, and the harness is public (apps/js-matrix, apps/wasm-matrix, wasm-kernels/kernels/matrix/src/lib.rs, tools/bench-runner/matrix-sweep.mjs). No CPU model, OS, or Chromium/V8 version is stated anywhere (docs/ENV.md is linked but absent from the repo), so it is first-party with partial methodology: tier C.

corrections.baseline: JavaScript matrix multiplication (same naive i-k-j loop over Float32Array, TypeScript served by the Vite dev server) in Chromium via Playwright; the matrix sweeps were run only in Chromium (npm scripts exist only for sweep:*-matrix:chromium); Firefox scripts exist only for the particle demo
corrections.claimed_speedup: Matrix multiply, median of 20 reps per size, Chromium, JS vs WASM in ms: 64x64 0.50 vs 0.50 (1.00x), 128x128 3.45 vs 2.20 (1.57x), 256x256 28.85 vs 15.65 (1.84x), 512x512 218.05 vs 136.10 (1.60x). On means (matrix_js_vs_wasm.csv) the speedups are 1.49x, 1.69x, 1.46x and 1.50x. P95 in WASM is 57-61% lower at n<=128 but 28-31% higher at n>=256. Particle physics step 1.7-2.8x faster in WASM, but frame rate is equal (about 60 FPS, GPU bound; frame-time ratio 1.01-1.10x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack build --target web --release (QUICKSTART asks for Rust >= 1.90.0, wasm-pack >= 0.13.1); no [profile.release] overrides in wasm-kernels/Cargo.toml or kernels/matrix/Cargo.toml, so Cargo release defaults (opt-level 3) plus wasm-pack's default wasm-opt pass; no simd128 target feature. JS side is TypeScript served unminified by the Vite 5 dev server; Playwright ^1.56 bundled Chromium, version not stated.
corrections.caveats: Harness bug: apps/wasm-matrix/src/wasm-bridge.ts passes the JS Float32Array to the Rust set_a/set_b(ptr: *const f32, len) exports via a 'buf as any as number' cast, so the pointer coerces to 0 and Rust copies len floats from linear-memory address 0 (UB on a null pointer in Rust) instead of the seeded matrices; the WASM side therefore multiplies different (probably mostly zero) data and its result is never compared with the JS result (only C[0] is read as a 'checksum'). The loop does the same n^3 scalar f32 multiply-adds, so timing is probably still representative, but the 'identical computation' claim does not hold. Other caveats: academic single-commit repo (master's thesis, Nov 2025); no licence (README says code is for academic and educational purposes), so reference only; CPU, OS and browser versions not given and docs/ENV.md is linked but missing; raw per-run results are gitignored, only aggregated CSV/MD are committed; each page load times 20 reps with no warm-up separation (JIT tier-up included); the 64x64 row sits at the 0.1 ms timer granularity; README figures are medians, means give 1.46-1.69x; naive O(n^3) kernel only, no SIMD on either side.

notes: Numbers on the page match the record (README table equals results/figures/matrix/matrix_results_table.md; medians). Shortcomings to record: WASM bridge passes a typed array as a raw pointer, so the Rust kernel reads its inputs from address 0 and multiplies different data than JS (result unchecked); no hardware or browser versions; no licence; single-commit thesis repo; matrix sweeps Chromium only.

tier_reason: First-party JetBrains charts (two PNGs in the kotlin-wasm-benchmarks README) compare Kotlin/Wasm against Kotlin/JS output in V8/Chrome; the benchmark code is public (Kotlin/kotlin-wasm-benchmarks src/, kotlinx-benchmark), but the charts state no CPU, engine version, Kotlin version or flags, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Relative-time bar chart (Kotlin/JS = 100%, lower is better), read off the screenshot by pixel position so approximate (derived from page data): List about 39% (about 2.5x faster), Queens about 64%, Bounce about 64%, CD about 66%, Sieve about 69%, Permute about 70%, Storage about 73%, Havlak about 77%, Towers about 77%, nBody about 80% (so roughly 1.25-1.6x faster), Mandelbrot about 102% (no gain), JSON about 174% (about 1.7x slower). Compose Multiplatform chart (JVM = 100%): Wasm about 156% / 181% / 158% vs JS about 329% / 399% / 315% on AnimatedVisibility / LazyGrid / VisualEffects, so Wasm about 2.0-2.2x faster than JS (derived from page data; Compose data from JetBrains/compose-multiplatform branch bench_with_kwasm).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Screenshots were committed 2023-12-07 (commit a82a6cb, Kotlin/Wasm Alpha era); the Kotlin, V8/Chrome and Binaryen versions used for them are not stated. JetBrains' December 2023 'Kotlin for WebAssembly goes Alpha' post says the results came from a recent Google Chrome (search snippet only). The current harness pins kotlin_version=2.3.20-RC (gradle.properties), Node 26.2.0, d8/V8 15.0.45 and Binaryen 129 (gradle/libs.versions.toml), with kotlin.js.ir.output.granularity=whole-program; README tasks wasmBenchmark, wasmOptBenchmark (Binaryen-optimised) and jsBenchmark; which Wasm variant the chart shows is not stated.
corrections.caveats: Numbers exist only as two PNG screenshots committed 2023-12-07, nearly three years old and predating Kotlin 2.x and current V8, so they may not reflect today's compiler; read by eye (+-3 points); no CPU, engine version, Kotlin version or warm-up settings stated; baseline is Kotlin/JS compiler output, not hand-written JS or TypeScript; README calls the suite work-in-progress; the benchmark repo's LICENSE.md lists Apache-2.0, BSD and MIT for different benchmark sources without mapping them; the compiler itself (JetBrains/kotlin) is Apache-2.0 per its README; JSON is about 1.7x slower and Mandelbrot is level, so the win is workload-dependent; the Compose chart comes from a separate compose-multiplatform benchmark branch; the entry id points at the whole Kotlin compiler repo, the Wasm backend being one part of it.

notes: Chart values match the record within reading error. Shortcomings to record: evidence is two first-party screenshots dated 2023-12-07 (Kotlin/Wasm Alpha) with no hardware or engine versions; Kotlin/JS output, not hand-written JS, is the baseline; JSON about 1.7x slower. Kotlin/kotlin-wasm-benchmarks: 23 stars, default branch dev, last commit 2026-10-07; JetBrains/kotlin 53.5k stars.

tier_reason: README numbers match exactly and the Rust drivers are public (src/main.rs native, src/main.js for the wasm build, benches/pathfinder.rs) with CPU (Ryzen 9 3900X) and release flags in Cargo.toml, but the TypeScript and AssemblyScript rows have no driver in the repo and come from earlier package versions, and Node/V8 versions are not stated, so the JS baseline is not reproducible: tier C.

corrections.baseline: TypeScript implementation of the same rsmod pathfinder on Node.js (the package's own 4.2.5 TypeScript release, commit 1114386, built with tsc); also the package's 5.0.x AssemblyScript WebAssembly release (commit 8ff4033)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Per call, 100k paths on the Lumbridge map square: Rust native about 2.8 us (278-281 ms per 100k); Rust WebAssembly on Node about 7.0 us (699-705 ms); AssemblyScript WebAssembly about 15.3 us (1519-1544 ms); TypeScript about 38.5 us (3820-3858 ms). So Rust wasm is about 5.5x and AssemblyScript wasm about 2.5x faster than TypeScript (derived from page data). Separately, cargo bench pathfinder/find_path (native Rust, criterion) reports 7.19 us, 2.6x slower than the native main.rs loop. README adds that the wasm build takes about 850 ms per 100k in a real server, without data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust: [profile.release] lto = true, opt-level = 3; wasm-pack release wasm-opt flags in Cargo.toml (--generate-global-effects --optimize-instructions --memory-packing --intrinsic-lowering --flexible-inline-max-function-size 4294967295 --inlining --inlining-optimizing -O4); wasm-pack build --target nodejs; native run in release on Windows x64. AssemblyScript 5.0.x: asc ^0.27.27 release target optimizeLevel 3, shrinkLevel 0, converge, noAssert, runtime minimal (asconfig.json at commit 8ff4033). TypeScript 4.2.5: tsc ^5.3.3, target esnext (tsconfig.json at commit 1114386). Rust, Node and V8 versions not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star, 5 forks; crates.io rsmod-pathfinder 2,620 total downloads (19 recent); npm @2004scape/rsmod-pathfinder downloads not re-checked (npm API blocked here)
corrections.caveats: Repository archived by the owner on 2026-02-17 (read-only); last commit 2024-10-26. The Rust drivers are in the repo (src/main.rs native, src/main.js loads dist/ from wasm-pack, timed with Date.now() over 100k calls), but the TypeScript and AssemblyScript rows have no driver at HEAD: they appear to measure the package's earlier 4.2.5 TypeScript and 5.0.x AssemblyScript releases (in git history), so the three implementations are different code versions and the TS/AS rows cannot be reproduced from HEAD. Node version not given. Synthetic single-map, single-route workload (destination 10 tiles north). The criterion bench (7.19 us native) disagrees with the native main.rs loop (2.8 us) without explanation; its iter_batched routine clones a PathFinder per iteration and drops it inside the timed region. The ~850 ms 'real world' figure is unexplained. First-party numbers.

notes: Record accurate on numbers, CPU, ISC licence and archived status; its caveat that main.js/main.rs are missing was wrong (both are in src/). Shortcomings to record: TypeScript and AssemblyScript baselines are earlier package releases with no driver at HEAD; Node version unstated; single synthetic route; archived 2026-02-17.
